records.title: Found by: loop assessment (L19).
records.description: Found by: loop assessment (L19). The result contract had no way to tell our own limits from the server's: scan-static recorded every permanent skip, its own unsupported languages, multi-server layouts, reader limits and reader errors included, as `no_runnable_artifact`, which reads as the subject's. In the first 50 live results, 16 were skips and most were ours. Skips may now carry `fault` (tool, subject, infra, policy); our limits have their own reasons (`unsupported_language`, `unsupported_layout`, `reader_limit`, `no_tools_found`, `too_large`, `tool_error`) that may only be the tool's; a skip without `fault` is read through a fixed map, with `unknown` for an ambiguous reason, never the subject.

test.name: R-COV-01: every skip reason has a fixed fault map; our own limits are reasons of their own and always the tool's
R-COV-01: a manifest without fault (an older worker kit) is valid; a declared fault must be one its reason allows
R-COV-01: skipFault and resultFault: declared first, then the fixed map; our limits win over every other side

records.title: Found by: loop assessment (L19).
records.description: Found by: loop assessment (L19). Ingest and the state store kept no fault side, so a tool-fault skip was stored like any other accepted result and could be counted as excluded or as the server's failure. Ingest now records each accepted result's fault and coverage state (`unassessed_tool` for our limits, never `excluded`), the state store keeps them (schema 7: `results.fault`, `results.coverage`, `results.assessed_at`), and a declared fault that its reason does not allow is `manifest_invalid`. The JSON ledger (`ingest/ledger.mjs`, `--ledger-json`) now also keeps an accepted result's `result_outcome` (`skips_only`), `fault` and `coverage`; it dropped `resultOutcome` before.

test.name: R-COV-02: a tool-fault skip is accepted and recorded as unassessed_tool, never as the subject's or excluded
R-COV-02: an older worker kit's bundle (no fault) is accepted; an ambiguous reason is recorded as unknown, a clear one by the fixed map
R-COV-02: a skip that puts our own limit down to the subject is rejected as manifest_invalid
R-COV-02: a rejected item carries no fault or coverage to the ledger (only accepted results are stored)
R-COV-02: the JSON ledger keeps an accepted result's fault side and coverage, and drops them from a refused one
R-COV-02: recordResult stores the fault side and coverage of an accepted result; a later skip keeps assessed_at
R-COV-02: ingest over the real store records a tool-fault skip as unassessed_tool
R-COV-02: migration from version 6 keeps results and adds fault, coverage and assessed_at as NULL

records.title: Found by: loop assessment (L19, gap 3).
records.description: Found by: loop assessment (L19, gap 3). The due list's coverage-gap priority was a stub (`coverageGap: () => 0`), so subjects never assessed, or whose last result was our own limit, got no priority for it. A due pair with no result yet, or never assessed and last hit a passing condition, or whose last result is our own limit and something moved since (R-COV-06), now gets `coverage_gap_share` (0.5) x its tier weight, capped below the tier above (R-COV-05). With equal reasons and age a boosted pair stays below a bare pair of the tier above. After a tool release, tool-fault skips are due again and, with equal age, first in their tier. A first-sight pair (no reason weight, no age) goes ahead of a stale pair of its tier only while the boost beats stale's 10 points plus the stale result's age: always in T0, in T1 while it is under 20 days old, never in T2 to T4.

test.name: R-COV-03: gapKind: never assessed, or last unassessed by our own limit once something moved; not the subject's side, policy or a result from before coverage
R-COV-03: the boost is coverage_gap_share x the tier weight (capped below the tier above), so it follows tier (popularity)
R-COV-03: within a tier, a never-assessed pair is boosted and a stale assessed one is not; the boost never makes a pair due
R-COV-03: a new tool version makes every tool-fault skip due again (tool_version), boosted ahead of the rest of its tier
R-COV-03: dueFromState reads fault and coverage from the store; an assessed result under an older run_key counts as assessed

records.title: The coverage-gap boost was not capped: at T2, 0.5 x 40 = 20 equalled the 20-point gap to T1, so a T2 tool-fault pair after a tool release (81) outranked a T1 assessed pair of the same age (80.5), and…

records.title: Two pulls into one archive at the same time (the agent and one started by hand) were not guarded against.
records.description: Two pulls into one archive at the same time (the agent and one started by hand) were not guarded against. A run now holds a `mkdir` lock in `<dest>/.lock`, exits 0 if a live run holds it, and takes over a lock whose pid is gone or that is over 12 hours old. The 12-hour rule for a lock on the same host was later superseded by R-ARC-12 (pid only on this host; 12 hours untouched only for another host's lock).

test.name: R-ARC-08: a second run while a live one holds the lock does nothing and exits 0
R-ARC-08: a lock from a dead run on this host, or from another host untouched for 12 hours, is taken over; a recent one from another host is not
R-ARC-08: the lock is released when a run fails part way

records.title: A run killed while writing left its `.partial-<id>-<pid>` folder in the archive for good.
records.description: A run killed while writing left its `.partial-<id>-<pid>` folder in the archive for good. Leftovers from dead pids are now removed when a run starts.

test.name: R-ARC-09: temporary folders left by a dead run are removed at start; a live run's are kept

records.title: NIT.
records.description: NIT. The `created_at ... is not a date` message never fired: `new Date(NaN).toISOString()` threw its own RangeError first. The time is now checked before it is formatted, and a bad time never becomes the cursor.

test.name: R-ARC-10: an ingest artifact whose created_at is not a date fails with that message

records.title: The inflated-size cap of `readZipLenient` did not bound the work: an entry was counted only after it passed, so entries that inflated and then failed their CRC cost a full inflate each, and many cent…
records.description: The inflated-size cap of `readZipLenient` did not bound the work: an entry was counted only after it passed, so entries that inflated and then failed their CRC cost a full inflate each, and many central-directory entries could point at the same local data. A 67 KB zip of 30 bad-CRC 64 MiB entries inflated 1.88 GiB under a 100 MB cap, reachable through an artifact a fork's pull request uploads. Every entry read now counts before it is inflated, pass or fail, and a local offset used twice is refused.

test.name: R-ARC-11: entries that fail after inflating still count toward the cap, and entries sharing local data are refused

records.title: A live run's lock on the same host was taken over once 12 hours old, though a first backfill at the API budget can take longer and a Mac that sleeps mid-run looks old.
records.description: A live run's lock on the same host was taken over once 12 hours old, though a first backfill at the API budget can take longer and a Mac that sleeps mid-run looks old. On this host a lock is now stale only when its pid is gone; from another host, when it has not been touched for 12 hours, and a run touches its lock after each artifact.

test.name: R-ARC-12: a live run on this host keeps its lock however long it runs; one on another host keeps it while it touches it

records.title: Two runs judging one lock stale at once could both take it over, the second removing the lock the first had just taken.
records.description: Two runs judging one lock stale at once could both take it over, the second removing the lock the first had just taken. A takeover now runs under its own `mkdir` guard, `.lock.takeover`, and only if the owner file still names the holder judged stale.

test.name: R-ARC-13: two runs cannot both take over one stale lock, nor take one another run has just taken

records.title: On a case-insensitive, normalising disk (APFS), `A.tar.age` and `a.tar.age`, or NFC and NFD forms of one name, are one file; `x/./y` and `a//b` pass the zip reader.
records.description: On a case-insensitive, normalising disk (APFS), `A.tar.age` and `a.tar.age`, or NFC and NFD forms of one name, are one file; `x/./y` and `a//b` pass the zip reader. Writing them failed with EEXIST, which was retried, so the artifact looped until it expired and was lost with no quarantine copy. Names are now compared folded, empty and `.` parts and any-case `.artifact.json` are refused, and a name the disk cannot write sends the whole download to quarantine.

test.name: R-ARC-14: names that one disk folds together, and empty or "." parts, are refused; a name the disk cannot write sends the whole download to quarantine

records.title: Index and manifest appends and the cursor were not durable: a power loss could keep a cursor past lines that never reached the disk.
records.description: Index and manifest appends and the cursor were not durable: a power loss could keep a cursor past lines that never reached the disk. Appends are now fsynced, and the cursor (and `.last-ok.json`) is replaced through a synced temporary file and rename, after the lines.

test.name: R-ARC-15: index and manifest lines are synced to disk, and the cursor is replaced whole only after them

records.title: Found by: review (present since the archive pull began).
records.description: Found by: review (present since the archive pull began). Nothing checked where an artifact came from, and a pull request from a fork can upload `ingest-*`, `history-*` or `registry-*` names. An artifact is now pulled only if its run is in this repository (not a fork), on `main`, and from the workflow that makes that kind; others are logged and left, not quarantined and not a failure.

test.name: R-ARC-16: an artifact not made by our own workflow on main is refused unread, not quarantined, and not a failure

records.title: NIT.
records.description: NIT. A quarantine found in its folder after a run died before indexing it was indexed as recovered but not reported, so no notification was shown. It now counts as quarantined.

test.name: R-ARC-17: a quarantine recovered after a run died before indexing it is still reported and notified

records.title: NIT.
records.description: NIT. An artifact whose `created_at` is not a date failed once, then was silently left out of every later run by the cursor's look-back filter. It is now kept in the list, so it keeps failing visibly.

test.name: R-ARC-18: an artifact whose created_at is not a date keeps failing visibly on later runs
R-ARC-10: an ingest artifact whose created_at is not a date fails with that message

records.title: The state asset is overwritten on every pump run and had no versioned copy (DESIGN-v3 §2, F6, promised one): a damaged or deleted asset would restart the loop from empty.
records.description: The state asset is overwritten on every pump run and had no versioned copy (DESIGN-v3 §2, F6, promised one): a damaged or deleted asset would restart the loop from empty. Hourly snapshots now keep the 48 newest copies and the newest of each UTC day for 30 days, counted in snapshots, not hours, so an idle loop never ages out what it relies on. Retention is now 24 newest, 14 daily and 8 weekly (loop upgrade #14).

test.name: R-SNAP-01: retention keeps the 24 newest, the newest of each UTC day for 14 days and of each UTC week for 8 weeks, and prunes the rest
R-SNAP-01: an idle loop prunes nothing: retention counts snapshots, not hours

records.title: Without dedupe an idle loop would fill the 48 hourly places with identical copies and push older, different states out.
records.description: Without dedupe an idle loop would fill the 48 hourly places with identical copies and push older, different states out. A run whose live sha256 equals the newest snapshot uploads nothing and only refreshes `current_at`; a return to an older state is a new snapshot.

test.name: R-SNAP-02: dedupe compares against the newest snapshot only
R-SNAP-02: an unchanged state uploads nothing but refreshes current_at
R-SNAP-02: a changed state is a new snapshot, and so is a return to an older state

records.title: A snapshot that does not read back intact is worse than none, since it is only found out during a restore.
records.description: A snapshot that does not read back intact is worse than none, since it is only found out during a restore. Each snapshot is checked against its manifest entry (sha256, size, name, age ciphertext); a new upload is downloaded back and checked before the manifest names it, and deleted if it fails.

test.name: R-SNAP-03: verifySnapshot accepts the bytes the manifest describes and refuses a changed byte, a wrong size, a wrong name or plaintext
R-SNAP-03: an upload that does not read back intact is deleted and the run fails

records.title: The snapshot runs outside the pump's concurrency group, so the pump can replace the asset while it is being copied.
records.description: The snapshot runs outside the pump's concurrency group, so the pump can replace the asset while it is being copied. The copy must match the asset's sha256 label and the asset must be unchanged (id, label, `updated_at`) after the download, else it is copied once more, then the run fails. An unlabelled or plaintext asset is never copied.

test.name: R-SNAP-04: the pump pushing during the copy is detected and the copy is retried once
R-SNAP-04: bytes that do not match the label, twice, fail the run and upload nothing
R-SNAP-04: an interrupted pump push (temporary name only) is copied like the pump would read it
R-SNAP-04: a plaintext or unlabelled state asset is never copied

records.title: A lost manifest or a failed delete must not lose or strand snapshots.
records.description: A lost manifest or a failed delete must not lose or strand snapshots. The manifest is reconciled with the assets on every run (missing entries rebuilt from name and label, stale entries dropped) and is written before any pruned asset is deleted.

test.name: R-SNAP-05: a lost manifest is rebuilt from the snapshot assets, and a stale entry is dropped
R-SNAP-05: pruned snapshots are deleted only after the manifest that drops them is written

records.title: The snapshot job copies a public ciphertext and must hold nothing more: only `contents: write`, no environment, no secrets, no age identity, never decrypts, and the kill switch first.
records.description: The snapshot job copies a public ciphertext and must hold nothing more: only `contents: write`, no environment, no secrets, no age identity, never decrypts, and the kill switch first.

test.name: R-SNAP-06: the snapshot workflow holds only contents: write, no secrets or key, and checks the kill switch first

records.title: There was no tested way to put a snapshot back.
records.description: There was no tested way to put a snapshot back. The drill verifies a snapshot against the manifest before decrypting it, decrypts locally without printing the key, runs `PRAGMA integrity_check` and reports the counts, and leaves no plaintext. `--apply` runs only while the loop is stopped and no pump or ingest run is active, snapshots the live state first, keeps the replaced asset renamed, and changes nothing if the live asset moves during the restore.

test.name: R-SNAP-07: inspectDatabase reports integrity, schema version, the fence and row counts, subjects and results first
R-SNAP-07: the drill verifies, decrypts and checks a snapshot with the age identity, and leaves no plaintext behind
R-SNAP-07: a snapshot whose bytes differ from the manifest is refused before it is decrypted
R-SNAP-07: a snapshot that decrypts to a damaged database fails the drill
R-SNAP-07: --apply needs the loop stopped: switched off, pump lane off, or paused for at least 10 more minutes
R-SNAP-07: --apply refuses while the loop runs or a pump run is active, and changes nothing
R-SNAP-07: --apply keeps the live state as a snapshot first, then puts the chosen snapshot back byte for byte
R-SNAP-07: --apply replaces a live asset that cannot be copied, and keeps it renamed
R-SNAP-07: --apply leaves the live state alone if it changes during the restore
R-SNAP-07: a snapshot that opens but fails PRAGMA integrity_check fails the drill with report.ok false

records.title: Snapshots that silently stop are found out only when one is needed.
records.description: Snapshots that silently stop are found out only when one is needed. The health item is amber when no run has confirmed the live state is captured for 3 hours (or there is no snapshot yet) and red after 6, measured from `current_at` so an idle loop stays green.

test.name: R-SNAP-08: the snapshot health item is green to 3 hours, amber to 6, red after
R-SNAP-08: age is measured from current_at, so an idle loop with running snapshots stays green
R-SNAP-08: no snapshot yet or an unreadable manifest is amber; a lane switched off is off

records.title: Nothing watched the snapshots: if the hourly run stopped (the GitHub schedule on this repository has not fired reliably), nobody would know until a restore was needed.
records.description: Nothing watched the snapshots: if the hourly run stopped (the GitHub schedule on this repository has not fired reliably), nobody would know until a restore was needed. The watchdog now puts a `state-snapshot` item on the health issue (amber after 3 hours, red after 6), and `state-snapshot.yml` is a loop workflow: a failed run is red and a workflow GitHub disabled for inactivity is turned back on.

test.name: R-SNAP-09: the watchdog shows the state snapshots on the health issue: amber after 3 hours, red after 6, off with the lane off
R-SNAP-09: the watchdog reads the snapshot manifest from the release with the job token; an unreadable one is amber, not a failed run
R-SNAP-09: state-snapshot.yml is a loop workflow: its failed run is red and its lane switch is read

records.title: A snapshot asset the manifest did not list was adopted on the word of its label, without a download: a failed read-back whose delete also failed (or a read-back that threw) left an orphan that became…
records.description: A snapshot asset the manifest did not list was adopted on the word of its label, without a download: a failed read-back whose delete also failed (or a read-back that threw) left an orphan that became the newest snapshot, so dedupe said unchanged, health said green, and the drill failed. Unlisted assets are now downloaded and verified first (deleted if they fail, left alone if unreadable), dedupe uses verified entries only, any read-back failure deletes the upload, and the drill checks an unlisted snapshot against its label.

test.name: R-SNAP-10: an asset the manifest does not list is verified before it is adopted; one that fails is deleted and never used for dedupe
R-SNAP-10: an unlisted asset that cannot be downloaded is left alone and not trusted
R-SNAP-10: a read-back that throws deletes the upload and fails the run
R-SNAP-10: the drill can use a snapshot the manifest does not list, checked against its own label

records.title: `restore --apply` kept only an asset named exactly `state.sqlite` and deleted every `state.sqlite.upload-*`.
records.description: `restore --apply` kept only an asset named exactly `state.sqlite` and deleted every `state.sqlite.upload-*`. After an interrupted pump push the live state is such an upload; with the pre-restore snapshot also failing, the live state would have been lost. The live asset itself, whatever its name, is now renamed to `state.sqlite.replaced-*`; only other stale uploads are deleted.

test.name: R-SNAP-11: --apply over an interrupted pump push keeps that upload (renamed), deletes only other stale uploads

records.title: `parseManifest` accepted any array: a null entry crashed every run, and an entry's `created` came from the manifest, so a future date pinned it as newest for good and broke dedupe.
records.description: `parseManifest` accepted any array: a null entry crashed every run, and an entry's `created` came from the manifest, so a future date pinned it as newest for good and broke dedupe. Every entry is now checked (snapshot name, a 64-hex sha256 the name carries), `created` always comes from the name, and snapshots dated in the future are left out.

test.name: R-SNAP-12: malformed manifest entries are left out, created always comes from the name, and a run does not crash on them
R-SNAP-12: a snapshot asset named in the future is left out of dedupe and retention

records.title: `restore --apply` read only the first 30 repository variables, and a `LOOP_ENABLED` it did not see counted as stopped: fail open.
records.description: `restore --apply` read only the first 30 repository variables, and a `LOOP_ENABLED` it did not see counted as stopped: fail open. It also ignored the `loop` environment, which overrides the repository for the pump job. The switches are now read as the pump sees them (environment, repository, every page of the organization variables shared with the repository), and any read error refuses.

test.name: R-SNAP-13: --apply refuses when the loop switches cannot be read
R-SNAP-13: the loop switches are read as the pump job sees them: environment, then repository, then every organization page

records.title: Active runs were only `in_progress` and `queued`, so a pending, waiting or requested pump run did not block `--apply`, and nor did a snapshot run in CI racing the restore's own snapshot.
records.description: Active runs were only `in_progress` and `queued`, so a pending, waiting or requested pump run did not block `--apply`, and nor did a snapshot run in CI racing the restore's own snapshot.

test.name: R-SNAP-14: a run that has not finished in any state blocks --apply, a snapshot run in CI included

records.title: Losing the copy race with the pump on both tries failed the run (red on the health issue) although nothing was wrong.
records.description: Losing the copy race with the pump on both tries failed the run (red on the health issue) although nothing was wrong. It now ends with a notice and exit 0; the staleness item reports it if it keeps happening. A download of an asset the pump just deleted counts as the same race.

test.name: R-SNAP-15: losing the race with the pump on both tries is a notice and exit 0, not a failed run

records.title: The snapshot health item could throw on a manifest with null entries, showed green for a `current_at` in the future, and said "no state snapshot yet" for a missing manifest.
records.description: The snapshot health item could throw on a manifest with null entries, showed green for a `current_at` in the future, and said "no state snapshot yet" for a missing manifest. It now never throws (amber instead), treats a time more than 5 minutes ahead as amber, and tells no release, no manifest and an empty manifest apart.

test.name: R-SNAP-16: a current_at more than 5 minutes in the future is amber, not green
R-SNAP-16: no release, no manifest and an empty manifest are told apart
R-SNAP-16: snapshotCheck never throws: null entries or a broken manifest object are amber

records.title: MEDIUM-LOW.
records.description: MEDIUM-LOW. A snapshot manifest with two or more null entries made the newest-snapshot sort throw, and `evaluate()` is not in a try, so the whole watchdog run failed and the health issue was not written. The parser now drops such entries (R-SNAP-12), `snapshotCheck` never throws (R-SNAP-16), and the watchdog fences it anyway: anything unexpected is an amber item. A missing release, a missing manifest and a time in the future are amber with their own wording.

test.name: R-SNAP-17: a snapshot manifest with null entries, one that throws, or a time in the future is amber; the watchdog run still writes the issue

records.title: A lock on this host whose pid had been reused (after a reboot the pid can belong to anything, even pid 1) was never taken over, so the archive stopped until someone removed it.
records.description: A lock on this host whose pid had been reused (after a reboot the pid can belong to anything, even pid 1) was never taken over, so the archive stopped until someone removed it. `owner.json` now records the host's boot time, and a lock from an earlier boot, or whose pid `ps` shows running something other than `archive-pull`, is stale. OPERATIONS says how to remove the lock by hand. Refined by R-ARC-23 and R-ARC-24: the pid's command line now decides first, and the boot time only when `ps` cannot tell.

test.name: R-ARC-19: a lock on this host from an earlier boot, or whose pid now runs another program, is taken over

records.title: Our own artifacts were refused silently when a workflow was renamed or added: one from this repository on `main` but from a workflow `SOURCES` did not list got a log line only, and the cursor moved p…
records.description: Our own artifacts were refused silently when a workflow was renamed or added: one from this repository on `main` but from a workflow `SOURCES` did not list got a log line only, and the cursor moved past it, so it was never archived. It is now held: a failure (exit 1, a notification, the cursor stays) until `SOURCES` lists the workflow; refusals of forks and other branches stay silent. A test maps every `upload-artifact` name prefix in `.github/workflows/` to `SOURCES`.

test.name: R-ARC-20: our own artifact from a workflow SOURCES does not list is held, retried and notified, not passed over
R-ARC-20: every artifact a workflow here uploads under an archived prefix is mapped in SOURCES to that workflow

records.title: NIT.
records.description: NIT. The provenance check looked every run up with its own request, which slows a first backfill of thousands of artifacts. With ten or more runs to check, runs now come from the run list 100 a page; a run the list does not show gets one request.

test.name: R-ARC-21: many runs are looked up from the run list a page at a time, with one GET for each run it does not find

records.title: Nothing on GitHub watched the archive heartbeat `ARCHIVE_LAST_OK`, so an archive that stopped was seen only on the Mac.
records.description: Nothing on GitHub watched the archive heartbeat `ARCHIVE_LAST_OK`, so an archive that stopped was seen only on the Mac. The watchdog now has an `archive` item, read from `${{ vars.ARCHIVE_LAST_OK }}` through `env:` (the job token cannot read variables through the API): amber after 12 hours or dated in the future, red after 24 hours or when empty, not JSON, or without a valid `at`.

test.name: R-ARC-22: the watchdog shows the archive heartbeat from vars.ARCHIVE_LAST_OK: amber after 12 hours, red after 24 or when it is empty or unreadable
R-ARC-22: watchdog.yml passes vars.ARCHIVE_LAST_OK to the watchdog step through env

records.title: macOS moves `kern.boottime` when the clock is set, so a wall-clock jump of more than 2 minutes made a live pull's lock look like one from an earlier boot, and a second run could take it over.
records.description: macOS moves `kern.boottime` when the clock is set, so a wall-clock jump of more than 2 minutes made a live pull's lock look like one from an earlier boot, and a second run could take it over. A live pid that is not ours and whose `ps` line contains `archive-pull.mjs` (or is the holder's recorded line, R-ARC-24) is now live whatever the boot time; the boot time decides only when `ps` cannot tell. The match is on `archive-pull.mjs`, not `archive-pull`, which a `tail -f` of the log also matched; `ps` runs with `-ww` so a line is never cut; a lock naming our own pid is stale.

test.name: R-ARC-23: a live archive pull keeps its lock across a clock jump; the boot time is used only when ps cannot tell

records.title: A pull started through a wrapper or a link without `archive-pull` in its command line had its live lock taken over.
records.description: A pull started through a wrapper or a link without `archive-pull` in its command line had its live lock taken over. `owner.json` now records the holder's own `ps` command line, and a pid still showing that line keeps the lock.

test.name: R-ARC-24: a run started through a wrapper or link records its own command line, and keeps its lock by it

records.title: Found by: loop tooling upgrades (item 10).
records.description: Found by: loop tooling upgrades (item 10). A release tag force-pushed to another commit was invisible: nothing recorded what each tag pointed to. meta-github now reads the newest 100 tags with their targets in its existing GraphQL batch (`git_tag_targets`, `git_tag_map_sha256`), and `longitudinal/derive.mjs` reports a version-like tag whose commit changed between two observations as a `git_tag_moves` event, ranked high.

test.name: R-DRIFT-01: a version-like release tag force-pushed to another commit is a git_tag_moves event, ranked high
R-DRIFT-01: meta-github records each tag's target (an annotated tag peeled once) and a hash of the tag map, in the same GraphQL batch

records.title: Found by: loop tooling upgrades (item 10).
records.description: Found by: loop tooling upgrades (item 10). An image tag that moved to a new image was invisible: the loop never recorded which digest a declared OCI tag resolved to. meta-registry now resolves up to five declared tags per subject with a manifest HEAD (`oci_tag_digests`), and a version-like tag with a new digest is an `oci_tag_moves` event, ranked medium (R-DRIFT-19).

test.name: R-DRIFT-02: a version-like image tag that resolves to a new digest is an oci_tag_moves event, ranked medium; latest moving is not
R-DRIFT-02: an image tag resolves to its digest with a manifest HEAD, one anonymous token per image, never a GET on docker.io

records.title: Found by: loop tooling upgrades (item 10).
records.description: Found by: loop tooling upgrades (item 10). A tool list that changed without a release had no signal. A changed tool list hash behind the same image digest is a `catalog_drift_same_version` event (`catalog_changed_same_image`, medium); behind a version tag that now points to a new digest, `catalog_changed_with_tag_move` (high).

test.name: R-DRIFT-03: a tool list that changes behind an unchanged image digest is a catalog_drift_same_version event; a new digest behind the same tag ranks high

records.title: Found by: loop tooling upgrades (item 10), false-positive guard.
records.description: Found by: loop tooling upgrades (item 10), false-positive guard. Floating tags (`latest`, `main`, `v1`, `1.2`) are meant to move. Only a full MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH tag, optionally v- or package-prefixed, can be an event; floating moves are counted, and a version tag re-annotated on the same commit is not a move.

test.name: R-DRIFT-04: version-like means a full MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, optionally v- or package-prefixed; floating tags are not
R-DRIFT-04: floating tags (latest, v1, v1.4, nightly, main) moving are counted, never events; a re-annotated version tag on the same commit is not a move

records.title: Found by: loop tooling upgrades (item 10), false-positive guard.
records.description: Found by: loop tooling upgrades (item 10), false-positive guard. Re-tagging minutes after a release is a common fix-up. A git tag whose old and new targets were made within an hour of each other, or an image tag whose old digest was last seen within an hour of the release, is kept but ranked low. The git dates are committer and tagger dates, which whoever made the commit or tag sets: they are not trusted alone, so a git move ranks low only when we also last saw the old target within an hour of when it was made (review).

test.name: R-DRIFT-05: the fix-up window is an hour either way between the two targets; unknown times rank high
R-DRIFT-05: a tag moved within an hour of its release is kept but ranked low (a fix-up re-tag), for git and for images
R-DRIFT-05: dates within the window rank low only when our own last sight of the old target was within the window of when it was made

records.title: Found by: loop tooling upgrades (item 10), false-positive guard.

records.title: Found by: loop tooling upgrades (item 10).
records.description: Found by: loop tooling upgrades (item 10). Tag names and image registry answers are upstream text that could pose as a result identity. The forgery controls now plant identity text in tag names, tag targets and an image answer's media type; tag names are sanitised before they are kept or hashed, and both controls stay contained.

test.name: R-DRIFT-09: tag names and image answers are upstream text: the forgery controls plant identity text in them and stay contained

records.title: Found by: loop tooling upgrades (item 10).
records.description: Found by: loop tooling upgrades (item 10). An image registry rate limit or outage must not be read as "no image". It is a retryable `oci` skip, the element keeps its status, and the host's remaining tags for that subject are not asked.

test.name: R-DRIFT-10: an OCI rate limit or outage is a retryable skip of the oci stage and stops further reads of that host only

records.title: A state asset that vanished (deleted by hand, a release cleaned up) made the pump start from an empty state and push it: every result, attempt and dispatch gone and the fence counter back to 0, with …
records.description: A state asset that vanished (deleted by hand, a release cleaned up) made the pump start from an empty state and push it: every result, attempt and dispatch gone and the fence counter back to 0, with the health issue green throughout. records.title: A worker run that completed inside its lease was rejected as `lease_expired` (which counts towards parking the run_key) whenever the pump only judged it after the lease ran out: the 150-second tick, …

records.description: A pump run that cannot read its state (damaged, encrypted to another key, from newer code, missing) still dispatched its successor first, so the chain ran a failing pump run about once a minute (about 70 an hour) until a person stepped in. A passing GitHub error while pulling is marked transient and keeps the chain going.

records.title: The loop's data lived only on GitHub (release assets; artifacts that expire after 30 or 90 days) and on the operator's Mac, so one account problem or one disk could lose it.
records.description: The loop's data lived only on GitHub (release assets; artifacts that expire after 30 or 90 days) and on the operator's Mac, so one account problem or one disk could lose it. `offsite-backup.yml` now copies the state snapshots, the snapshot manifest, the ingest artifacts and the history artifacts to an R2 bucket every 6 hours, byte for byte and never decrypted, under keys by kind and UTC day, with a manifest part and a cursor per run.

test.name: R-OFF-01: copies snapshots, the snapshot manifest, ingest and history artifacts byte for byte under kind/day keys, with a manifest part and a cursor
R-OFF-01: snapshot keys and artifact keys are by kind and UTC day

records.title: The bucket lock refuses overwrites for 30 days, and a copy that rewrote a key could lose the only good off-site copy.
records.description: The bucket lock refuses overwrites for 30 days, and a copy that rewrote a key could lose the only good off-site copy. A key that already holds the same sha256 is skipped by HEAD, without a download; one that holds other bytes is never overwritten: the copy goes beside it as `<key>.sha256-<12 hex>` and that run reports a verification failure.

test.name: R-OFF-02: dedupe: a second run copies nothing new; a key with the same sha256 is skipped by HEAD without a download; other bytes under a key are never overwritten

records.title: An upload that R2 stored differently would go unnoticed.
records.description: An upload that R2 stored differently would go unnoticed. Every PUT carries Content-MD5, x-amz-checksum-sha256 and the sha256 as metadata, and a HEAD after it must show the same size, an ETag equal to the MD5 and the same sha256; otherwise the run fails (`verify_failed`, red) and the cursor holds.

test.name: R-OFF-03: a HEAD after the PUT that does not show the bytes sent is a verification failure: red status, exit code 1, and the cursor holds

records.title: R2 has no spending cap, so a growing loop could pass the free tier silently.
records.description: R2 has no spending cap, so a growing loop could pass the free tier silently. Each run sums the whole bucket first and uploads nothing past `OFFSITE_MAX_BYTES` (default 8 GB, never above the 10 GB free tier): `over_cap`, red. Per-run byte and Class A/B operation caps stop a run early and leave the rest to the next, with the run's own manifest and cursor still written.

test.name: R-OFF-04: the cost cap: nothing is uploaded past OFFSITE_MAX_BYTES (status over_cap); per-run byte and operation caps defer to the next run

records.title: A pull request from a fork can upload an artifact with any name, so the name alone would let anyone put data into the backup.
records.description: A pull request from a fork can upload an artifact with any name, so the name alone would let anyone put data into the backup. The backup applies archive-pull's origin check (this repository, main, the workflow SOURCES lists): foreign artifacts are never downloaded; ours from an unlisted workflow are held and the cursor holds.

test.name: R-OFF-05: the origin filter: artifacts from a fork, another branch or another workflow are never copied; ours from an unlisted workflow are held

records.title: Without a cursor each run would list every artifact and judge every key again.
records.description: Without a cursor each run would list every artifact and judge every key again. A cursor object per run (the newest wins; the lock forbids rewriting one) makes the next run list back only to an hour before it and download only what is new; a kind with nothing in a complete listing starts from the run time.

test.name: R-OFF-06: the cursor: the next run lists artifacts only back to an hour before it, and downloads only what is new

records.title: The workflow had to merge before the R2 token exists.
records.description: The workflow had to merge before the R2 token exists. test.name: R-OFF-07: missing R2 settings: exit 0, an unconfigured heartbeat, no store and no GitHub call; the workflow keeps the secrets in the backup step

records.title: An R2 error message could carry the access key or account ID into a public log or heartbeat.
records.description: An R2 error message could carry the access key or account ID into a public log or heartbeat. A failed bucket read is an `error` heartbeat, not a crash, and the credentials and account ID are scrubbed from the heartbeat and every log line.

test.name: R-OFF-08: a failed bucket read is an error heartbeat, not a crash, and the credentials never reach the heartbeat

records.title: Nothing would show a stopped off-site backup.
records.description: Nothing would show a stopped off-site backup. The job token cannot write a repository variable, so each run uploads a heartbeat artifact and the watchdog reads the newest one from a trusted `offsite-backup.yml` run on main: green under 12 hours, amber to 24, when not configured, near the cap or stopped early; red after 24, over the cap or on a verification failure; off with the lane off.

R-OFF-09: the watchdog trusts only heartbeats from offsite-backup.yml runs on main in this repository, scheduled or dispatched
R-OFF-09: the watchdog run pushes the offsite item and watchdog.yml passes the lane switch

records.description: A bucket at the cap stops the backup, and a careless prune could delete the newest state snapshots. A local S3 stand-in checks the real client's PUT carries If-None-Match: *, Content-MD5, x-amz-checksum-sha256 and the sha256 metadata, that HEAD and LIST read them back, that a taken key is `exists`, and that errors carry no credentials.

records.title: (1) `vars.R2_ACCOUNT_ID` in a step's `env:` is printed in the public run log (only secrets are masked); it now comes from a secret when set.
records.description: (1) `vars.R2_ACCOUNT_ID` in a step's `env:` is printed in the public run log (only secrets are masked); it now comes from a secret when set. (2) ubuntu-slim stops jobs at 15 minutes, before a paced backfill could write its cursor; the job runs on ubuntu-24.04 and a run stops taking items after 30 minutes. (3) A PUT stored but answered `exists` on the SDK's retry was counted as `already`: the cap was undercounted and no manifest line was ever written. (4) A run that died before its manifest part left copies with no line; the next run now writes them, marked `recovered`. (5) Snapshot bytes counted against the artifacts' run budget and ingest past it stopped history; the budget is per phase and per kind. (6) One failed run with no last good time showed red at once; the watchdog takes it from an older heartbeat. (7) The prune ran after a cancelled run.

R-OFF-12: a run that failed before reading the bucket takes its last good time from an older heartbeat: amber, not red
R-OFF-07: missing R2 settings: exit 0, an unconfigured heartbeat, no store and no GitHub call; the workflow keeps the secrets in the backup step

records.title: (1) The `vars.R2_ACCOUNT_ID` fallback would print the account ID in the public log's env header (a repository variable of that name exists); it is now read only from `secrets`.
records.description: (1) The `vars.R2_ACCOUNT_ID` fallback would print the account ID in the public log's env header (a repository variable of that name exists); it is now read only from `secrets`. (2) A dispatch from another branch would get the R2 secrets; both jobs now run only on `refs/heads/main`. (3) Prune apply trusted any listing: one cut short (truncated with no token, or missing the newest cursor or run manifest) could make it delete from a wrong total; it now refuses, as it does with no cursor at all, and the backup treats such a page as an error. (4) SDK retries were not counted against the per-run operation caps, and a PUT whose every attempt failed was not counted against the size cap though it may have been stored; the client no longer retries, meter() retries and counts each attempt, and such bytes count as possibly stored. (5) The prune step summary was not scrubbed.

test.name: R-OFF-13: the account ID only from a secret, both jobs only on main; retries count against the operation caps; a PUT that failed every attempt counts as possibly stored; a truncated listing is an error
R-OFF-13: apply refuses a listing that looks cut short, and the step summary never shows the credentials
R-OFF-07: missing R2 settings: exit 0, an unconfigured heartbeat, no store and no GitHub call; the workflow keeps the secrets in the backup step

records.title: Found by: re-review of #35.
records.description: Found by: re-review of #35. The floating-word check (R-DRIFT-18) also matched words inside a package prefix, so `mcp-server-dev-tools@1.0.0`, `edge-runtime-v2.0.0`, `mcp-main@1.0.0` and `main-server-v1.0.0` counted as floating, and a real force-push of any of them would never be reported. A link or a second name is refused, and the file is opened with O_NOFOLLOW.

test.name: R-DRIFT-26: an --out that is a link, or a second name, for a file in the folder being read is refused and the file is untouched

records.title: Found by: review of #41.
records.description: Found by: review of #41. When a prune pass gave up a staged state archive (not on its run after 6 hours, or not readable) it staged a new one in the same run and recorded status `staged`, so the watchdog's `state-size` item stayed green. A broken upload step or archive read path would have staged, waited and given up for ever with nothing deleted and no alarm until the 256 MiB size threshold. Give-ups are now counted (kv `state.prune.giveups`) until a pass deletes rows, and the item is amber while any are counted.

test.name: R-PRUNE-01: an archive given up and staged again in the same run keeps the state-size item amber until a pass deletes again

records.title: Found by: review of #41.
records.description: Found by: review of #41. `attempts` and `slot_ledger` use `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` without AUTOINCREMENT, so pruning the newest row (a loop idle for over 7 days) let SQLite hand its id out again: two different attempts would share an id across the state archives. The live state was not at risk (deletes compare whole rows). The row with the highest id now always stays.

test.name: R-PRUNE-02: the newest attempt and slot row always stay, so their ids are never handed out again

records.title: Found by: review of #41.
records.description: Found by: review of #41. Only a missing artifact or one that failed read-back led to a give-up: an archive over the size cap, or a fetch that always failed (a token or download error), kept the staged note for ever, so nothing new was staged and pruning stalled until a person deleted the note. An oversized archive is now given up at once, and a fetch that fails six times (or for four times the give-up age) is given up.

test.name: R-PRUNE-03: an archive too big to read is given up at once, and one whose fetch keeps failing is given up after a few runs

records.title: Found by: review of #41 (G10, G8).
records.description: Found by: review of #41 (G10, G8). A test gap, not a fault found in the code: the 21-day equivalence tests never had a dispatch that straddles the prune cutoff (an item reported, or an ingest failure noted, before it; the dispatch closed after it; newer attempts so it is not the highest id), and `observe()` left out the `ingest.failures:*` counters. Both are now covered directly: the attempt and the counter stay with their kept dispatch, `getAttempt` still sees the outcome, a repeat is still a duplicate, and only the old dispatch's rows go.

test.name: R-PRUNE-04: an attempt received before the cutoff stays while its dispatch closed after it, even when it is not the highest id
R-PRUNE-04: ingest failure counters stay with a dispatch that straddles the cutoff and go with one that does not

records.title: COSMETIC.
records.description: COSMETIC. Found by: review of #41. A republished package with a modified `lib/index.js` that was in the git tree was silenced: any file in the source but different, under `lib/`, `dist/`, `build/`, `out/` or `release/`, was explained as `build_output_stale`. A file the source tree has with other content is now always `content_differs`; only a file the source lacks is build output. The version-stamp check (`onlyVersionLines`) accepted any differing line that said "version" or held an x.y.z; a line now counts only when it carries the artifact's version and is the same as the source's line once the version in each is blanked.

test.name: R-RD-06: a republished file that the source tracks and that differs is content_differs, even under lib/ or dist/
R-RD-06: a version stamp is a line whose only difference is the version, not any line that says "version" or holds a number

records.title: Found by: review of #37.
records.description: Found by: review of #37. A renamed repository answered 3xx and the lane did not follow: the subject ended as `source_repository_not_found`, `source_redirected` or `artifact_redirected` with no skip and no fault side, and a 403 or 429 from GitHub (throttling) was read as `not_found`, blaming the subject. A repository that moved is now read again at its new github.com name (three hops, host-checked) and its source comes from there; one that cannot be followed, a redirected codeload or download, is a retryable skip with fault tool; 403 and 429 are retryable skips with fault infra; every skip of the lane now says its fault side. Only a 404 (GitHub's 401 for a gone repository) is the subject's, and it stays data.

test.name: R-RD-07: a renamed repository is read at its new github.com name; one that moved elsewhere, a 403 and a 429 are skips with a fault side

records.title: Found by: review of #37.
records.description: Found by: review of #37. For each absent `.so`, `.pyd` or `.dll` the lane scanned the whole source tree (artifact files x tree entries), and the folder vote, the compiled-source check and the doc check did the same over every path with the same name, so a large monorepo could run a subject past the job time. Lookups are now indexed once per tree (path suffixes, folders holding native source, folder and file name pairs), and a compute budget of 90 seconds over all of a subject's comparisons ends it with a `reader_limit` skip (stage `compute_budget`, fault tool, not retried) and the outcome `compute_budget`.

test.name: R-RD-08: native, source and doc lookups are indexed (a large tree with many absent .so files compares in well under a second)
R-RD-08: the compute deadline ends the comparison (ComputeBudget) and the subject with a tool-fault skip, not a job timeout

records.title: Found by: review of #37.
records.description: Found by: review of #37. Registry JSON (npm, PyPI, deps.dev, the MCP registry) was read with redirects followed, and the host guard checked only the first URL, so an answer could send the lane off the allowed hosts. The lane now asks for manual redirects, follows one to another allowed address (at most two hops, each target checked again) and refuses anything else as `redirect_refused`, a retryable skip with fault tool.

test.name: R-RD-09: registry JSON reads do not follow redirects: one off the allowed hosts is refused, one to an allowed host is followed once checked

records.title: Found by: review of #37.
records.description: Found by: review of #37. Downloads of up to 120 seconds were retried twice, which could use up the 6-minute budget of a subject on one artifact, and the budget was checked only before a download, so registry, deps.dev and tag reads went on after it. Downloads are tried once, and the budget is checked before every network call; a subject past it makes one `reader_limit` skip and its unread packages are `subject_time_budget`.

test.name: R-RD-10: a download is tried once (no retries on a 120 s read), and the subject budget applies before every network call

records.title: Found by: review of #37.
records.description: Found by: review of #37. Any archive error became a public finding: a zip entry with a compression method our reader lacks, an encrypted entry, a zip64 archive or a tar number our parser cannot hold gave `artifact_unreadable` (medium) or `unsafe_entry_refused` (high) about a package that may be fine. These are now reader limits (a `reader_limit` skip with fault tool, outcome `reader_limit`). Findings stay for a zip or tar that is damaged (cut short, bad checksum, bad gzip) and for entries whose names are unsafe.

test.name: R-RD-11: an archive our readers cannot read (unsupported zip method, zip64, a huge tar number) is a tool-fault skip, not a finding; real damage still is

records.title: Found by: review of #37.

test.name: R-RD-12: the held list is capped like the findings, with a last entry that counts what it left out, and held files stay out of public counts

records.title: Found by: re-review of #37.
records.description: Found by: re-review of #37. A GitHub 403 for a repository taken down (DMCA, disabled by GitHub staff) was read as throttling, so the subject was a retryable infra skip for ever. The 403 is now read by its headers and body: a rate-limit header (`x-ratelimit-remaining: 0`, `retry-after`) or a primary or secondary limit message is throttling (retried); a DMCA or disabled body, or a 451, means the repository is gone: a settled skip (`upstream_unavailable`, fault subject, not retryable) with the outcome `source_repository_gone` or `source_gone`. A 403 that says neither is still throttling.

test.name: R-RD-18: a 403 for a DMCA-blocked or disabled repository is a settled skip (upstream_unavailable, fault subject, not retryable); throttling stays a retryable infra skip

records.title: Found by: re-review of #37.
records.description: Found by: re-review of #37. An artifact whose bytes did not match the registry's digest was skipped as `upstream_unavailable` (fault infra, retryable), though it can be a real tamper. It is now a held finding in `release_diff_held` (class S, private: package, version, artifact, size, the sha256 of what was read, rule id `integrity_mismatch`), with no skip; the public artifact record is identical to that of an artifact the registry answers 404 for (`artifact_not_found`, no skip, no finding).

test.name: R-RD-19: an artifact whose bytes do not match the registry's digest is a held finding (not a retryable infra skip), and the public record does not say so

records.title: `forbiddenKind` matched "access blocked" and "has been disabled" anywhere in a 403 body, so other text containing those words (a release note, a package text) could be read as a repository taken down.
records.description: `forbiddenKind` matched "access blocked" and "has been disabled" anywhere in a 403 body, so other text containing those words (a release note, a package text) could be read as a repository taken down. The patterns are now GitHub's own repository-level messages ("Repository access blocked", "This repository has been disabled", "Access to this repository has been disabled"), anchored to the start of a line (after an optional "remote: ") or of the JSON "message"; the DMCA reason is read from `block.reason` or the anchored message.

test.name: R-RD-20: forbiddenKind reads only GitHub's own repository-level messages (start of a line or of the JSON message) as a repository taken down; the same words inside other text are not

records.title: Found by: the 25 Nov 2026 GitHub outage (15:55 to 16:36 UTC).
records.description: Found by: the 25 Nov 2026 GitHub outage (15:55 to 16:36 UTC). Every GitHub call in the loop had its own retry or none: the pump's REST client tried 4 times in about 7 seconds, the state asset client never repeated a POST, the snapshot client repeated nothing it posted. One burst of HTTP 500 on the successor dispatch broke the pump chain. One policy now (`pump/retry.mjs`): HTTP 500, 502, 503, 504, 429, a 403 with a rate-limit signal and network errors or timeouts are retried; any other 4xx is not. Up to 6 attempts, exponential delay with full jitter (2 s base, 120 s cap), `Retry-After` honoured up to 60 s (a longer one ends the retries), bounded by a total-sleep cap and an absolute deadline; each retry is logged (call, attempt n/6, reason, delay) with no token.

test.name: R-CHAOS-13: only 500, 502, 503, 504, 429, network errors and rate-limited 403s are transient; other 4xx are final
R-CHAOS-13: the delay is exponential with full jitter: base 2 s, doubling, cap 120 s
R-CHAOS-13: Retry-After is honoured and capped at 60 s; a longer one ends the retries
R-CHAOS-13: the retrier stops at the attempt limit, the total-sleep limit and the deadline, and logs each retry

records.title: Found by: the 25 Nov 2026 outage (HTTP 500 and 502 on the state asset upload).
records.description: Found by: the 25 Nov 2026 outage (HTTP 500 and 502 on the state asset upload). A state push stopped at the first server error, and a plain repeat of an upload that GitHub had stored would have failed as `already_exists` or left two copies. The state asset and snapshot clients now repeat an upload only after reading the release: a complete asset of that name with the same size and label is the upload and is used as it is, a partial or different one is deleted first. The unchanged-remote checks of the push (fencing) still run on the result, so a retried push cannot overwrite newer state. A release create is looked up before it is repeated.

test.name: R-CHAOS-14: a push whose upload gets HTTP 500 and 502 is repeated until it lands, with backoff, and logs the retries

records.description: Found by: design of R-CHAOS-13. Retries must not make a run overrun its job's timeout-minutes or hold on past the run's deadline. records.title: Found by: design (loop project item "Lane version pins are labels only: workers run ref main").
records.description: Found by: design (loop project item "Lane version pins are labels only: workers run ref main"). A lane's `versions.tool` and `versions.probe` go into every run_key, but the pump dispatched each worker on its branch (`ref: main`), so a result filed under a pin could have run whatever was on the worker's main: the label could lie. The pump now sends a lane's own pinned commit as `tool_sha` on a `pin_check: enforce` lane (a pin it cannot resolve is not dispatched), and ingest checks every bundle's manifest `tools` against the run_key's pins: another version is refused as `pin_mismatch` on every lane, an unproven one as `pin_unverified` on an enforce lane (accepted with a note on a `label` lane, the rollout setting). Tool fault side, not counted towards parking, lane paused for an hour. Mutation-checked: 13 protections turned off one at a time, each caught.

records.title: Found by: review of every recorded start failure (26 Nov).
records.description: Found by: review of every recorded start failure (26 Nov). 37 of the 38 PyPI `start_failed` results (fault `subject`) were not crashes in the server's own code: 27 a dependency that changed after the release (mcp 2.x removed `mcp.server.fastmcp`), 5 an extra we did not install, 2 a read-only site-packages, 1 a missing `libGL.so.1`, 1 macOS-only (`xcrun`), 1 a configuration request raised with a traceback. All 6 OCI `start_failed` were our forced `/tmp` workdir. `CRASH_TEXT` took any traceback or import error as the server's crash. `failureDetail` now names our sandbox, the platform, the network, extras and drift first; only a failed import of the server's own module (its wheel's top-level modules, or one named like the package) can still be `start_failed`. Replaying the 198 recorded start-failure results: subject-fault 87 to 11. A second review of #49 found Go and glibc messages in lower case (`read-only file system`, `no such host`), GitPython's `Bad git executable`, an unbuilt native addon, a bare CommonJS dependency that is not installed, a namespace folder (`google/`) counted as the server's own module, and a declared variable turning a crash of the server's own into `needs_credentials`; all fixed, and the replay of the 198 then gives subject-fault 11 (7 `needs_credentials` that are the server's own configuration messages, 4 `start_failed` that are crashes of its own code).

test.name: R-LP-59: of the 26 Nov PyPI start_failed results, only the crash in the server's own code is blamed on it

records.title: Found by: second review of #49.
records.description: Found by: second review of #49. Routing every failed import to our side sent real packaging defects of the server to `tool`: a submodule of its own package its wheel lacks (`stratevo.cli.commands`), and a module its own code imports that is not installed, not in its wheel and not in `requires_dist` (`httpx`, a `utils` left out). With the release's facts read and the importing frame in its own package or console script, these are `missing_own_module` and `undeclared_dependency` (`timeout_start`, fault `subject`). A module declared in base but missing (a failed install), one only an extra brings or that a server extra (`mcp`, `server`, `cli`) we did not install may bring transitively (FinanceToolkit's `[mcp]` brings `anyio` through `mcp`: `start_needs_extra`), Python's own or the venv's (3.11's stdlib list, which holds what 3.12 and 3.13 removed, plus setuptools, pkg_resources, pip, wheel), one imported from inside a dependency, or no facts: still ours.

test.name: R-LP-68: the server's own packaging defects stay the server's: a module of its own package its wheel lacks, a module its own code imports that it neither ships nor declares

records.title: Found by: second review of #49.
records.description: Found by: second review of #49. Sound, quick exits with a traceback were still `start_failed` for: an unset variable read (`KeyError: 'GITHUB_TOKEN'`), pydantic settings validation (`validation error for Settings`, `Field required`), a missing file at an absolute path (`FileNotFoundError ... '/data/index.json'`, Node `ENOENT ... open '/config/...'`), a full disk (`[Errno 28]`, `ENOSPC`), `KeyboardInterrupt` (our stop), and a crash whose last frame is inside an installed dependency (a SyntaxError or `X|Y` TypeError of a Python version it does not support). The first two are `start_needs_config`, the rest `start_env_limited` (tool); a crash whose last frame is the server's own code, or Python's library it called, stays `start_failed`. The mutation check covers the new `frame` rule.

test.name: R-LP-69: an unset variable read, pydantic settings, a missing absolute path, a full disk, our stop, or a crash inside a dependency is never the server's
R-LP-65: mutation check: with a start rule switched off its fixture gets another detail, and with all of them off every fixture is blamed on the server again

test.name: R-LP-71: a declared dependency whose import name differs from its distribution's is not undeclared when missing; an unknown mapping is ours

records.title: Found by: second review of #52.
records.description: Found by: second review of #52. `exitOf` took the sandbox's record of an HTTP-mode server's container at face value, so our own stop (`docker stop`, 143), our interrupt (130, with a `KeyboardInterrupt` traceback) or a segfault under the runtime (139) read as the server's own exit and, with a traceback, as `start_failed`. An exit of 128+n is now signal n over HTTP and stdio alike (never the server's own exit). test.name: R-LP-70: an exit of 128+n is signal n (our stop 143, our interrupt 130, a segfault 139), never the server's own exit; an image the sandbox would not run as is stays ours

records.title: Nothing measured how often mcp-check is fooled, and nothing stopped a release when a check started missing what it used to find: no ground-truth cases, no precision or recall per check and language (…
records.description: Nothing measured how often mcp-check is fooled, and nothing stopped a release when a check started missing what it used to find: no ground-truth cases, no precision or recall per check and language (design §10.2). Now `bench/` scores every case against its truth, and the required `bench` job of `ci.yml` fails when a check's false negatives rise or its recall falls below the baseline interval.

test.name: R-BENCH-01: the gate fails when a check's false negatives rise, or its recall drops below the baseline interval

records.description: A scorer that only echoed its labels would have looked perfect: nothing proved it reads mcp-check's output. Faulty-oracle cases (labels wrong on purpose) must each come out as a disagreement, or the run and the gate fail.

test.name: R-BENCH-02: a faulty-oracle label is reported as a disagreement, never echoed as a pass

records.title: The ~200 mcp-check mutants of design §4.6 did not exist, so nothing showed that the cases would catch a broken reader or check.
records.description: The ~200 mcp-check mutants of design §4.6 did not exist, so nothing showed that the cases would catch a broken reader or check. `bench/mutate.mjs` runs about 170 source and 42 fixture mutants weekly and on reader or check changes (`bench-mutants.yml`), and fails when a mutant on the kill list survives.

records.description: Found by: review of #31. test.name: R-BENCH-04: every core check has labelled positives: at least 3 in 2 languages for each security check, at least 1 for the others

records.title: Found by: review of #31.
records.description: Found by: review of #31. The gate only warned on false-positive rises: a bug raising `spec-name-charset` on 111 tools passed, and 11 of 50 ground-truth-killed mutants passed the required gate. records.title: Found by: review of #31.

records.title: Found by: review of #31.

records.title: Found by: bench (`python/docstring-unicode-escape`, `python/poison-escapes`).
records.description: Found by: bench (`python/docstring-unicode-escape`, `python/poison-escapes`). Python strings read `\uXXXX` as the letters `uXXXX` and did not decode `\xHH`, `\UXXXXXXXX` or octal (docstrings, `description=` and `name=` alike), so bidi, zero-width, tag and ANSI characters written as escapes never reached the poisoning checks, and `lookup_\u0430ccount` came out as `lookup_u0430ccount` (homoglyph missed, phantom name). Escapes are now decoded as Python decodes them; an unknown escape keeps its backslash; raw strings stay raw. Review follow-up: in a raw f-string a backslash no longer hides a `{expression}`.

test.name: R-RD-07: Python string escapes are decoded as Python decodes them (\x, \u, \U, octal); an unknown escape keeps its backslash
R-RD-07: a docstring written with \u escapes keeps the bidi characters they stand for, and the security check sees them
R-RD-07: a name= keyword is decoded, so a look-alike letter written as an escape is the name the server lists
R-RD-07: in a raw f-string a backslash stays and does not hide a {expression}

R-RD-08: the same name registered twice outside one literal array is still one tool (alternatives, not a list)
R-RD-08: duplicates in a literal array of another file than the name's first registration are not kept

records.title: Found by: bench (`typescript/factory-function`).
records.description: Found by: bench (`typescript/factory-function`). records.title: Found by: bench (`typescript/loop-over-definitions`).
records.description: Found by: bench (`typescript/loop-over-definitions`). `for (const t of TOOLS) server.registerTool(t.name, …)` reported one unresolved registration even though every name in `TOOLS` was read. Registrations in a loop over a literal or constant collection read in full are now read once per element; a loop over anything else still counts as unresolved. Review follow-up: only a const of the file that nothing changes is unrolled (a `push`, a reassigned `let`, an index assignment or a call taking it keep the registration unresolved); parameters and outer loop variables hide same-named constants; an index before `.forEach` is not a literal; a body that may `continue`, `break`, `return` or `throw` first is not unrolled; constants are overlaid, not copied per element (3,000 loops beside 4,000 constants took several seconds), and the work is charged to the file's budget.

test.name: R-RD-15: a for-of loop over a table whose names are all read leaves no unresolved registration
R-RD-15: a loop over a collection the reader does not know in full still counts its registration as unresolved
R-RD-15: a collection that is changed after its declaration (push, let reassigned, index assignment) is not unrolled; its registration stays unresolved
R-RD-15: a parameter or an outer loop variable that shadows a constant is not read as the constant
R-RD-15: an index expression before .forEach is not an array literal, and a loop body that may skip the registration is not unrolled
R-RD-15: many loops and factory calls next to many constants are read in linear time

records.title: Found by: loop upgrade 19 design (hostile-input rule).
records.description: Found by: loop upgrade 19 design (hostile-input rule). The ANSI and shell-URL scans use bounded quantifiers and one pass over scheme tokens; 200 KB of nested `a://`, `$`, backticks, `;`, ESC and OSC runs is read in linear time. Review of #37: the trailing-punctuation strip (`/[…]+$/`) was quadratic on a long run of `;` `.` `?` `*` followed by a letter (100,000 `;` then `a`: 5.9 s); it is now a backwards loop and R-CHK-04 covers those runs.

test.name: R-CHK-04: ANSI and shell-URL scans read hostile input in linear time

records.title: Found by: review of #37.
records.description: Found by: review of #37. Command words are now lowercase and need an argument; only `$(`, a bare `;`, `|` or `&&` start a shell line.

test.name: R-CHK-05: a newline after a URL fires only before shell syntax (case-sensitive command words, no fence, quote, paren or price)

records.title: live-probe oracle judge (new in this lane, found by its self test on GitHub before merge).
records.description: live-probe oracle judge (new in this lane, found by its self test on GitHub before merge). The Go SDK client writes `idempotentHint: false` on a tool whose annotations leave it out (the spec default), so on kronicle-lite 0.10.2 its catalog hash differed from our reader's and the other three clients', and the judge raised two D4 `schema_mismatch` leads that would have fired on most servers with annotations. Catalogs are now also compared with the annotations that only state the spec default removed; such a client is recorded as `catalog_vs_reader: same_but_annotation_defaults`, with no disagreement.

test.name: R-ORC-01: a client SDK that writes out an annotation default (Go: idempotentHint false) is the same catalog, not a D4 disagreement; a real difference still is

records.title: live-probe oracle stage (found from its self test on GitHub before merge).
records.description: live-probe oracle stage (found from its self test on GitHub before merge). The stage runs inside the sandbox driver's probe option, and the driver times its probe around that call, so `step_telemetry.probe_ms` held the oracle stage too (mcp-check: 12.4 s, of which about 1.2 s was the probe). The bundle now records `oracle_ms` and takes it out of `probe_ms`. The driver's own container record for the probe (raw telemetry) still spans both; corpus/LIVE-PROBE.md says so.

test.name: R-ORC-02: the driver's probe time holds the oracle stage (it runs inside the probe option); step_telemetry keeps the two apart

records.title: live-probe oracle stage (review, before merge).
records.description: live-probe oracle stage (review, before merge). A server could put a string of its choosing into `sdk_client_results.protocol_negotiated` and the results and control files outside raw/: the TypeScript 1.x client took the first `protocolVersion` in any message (a stray response with an unknown id is ignored by the SDK but was read by our tap), and the judge passed any 40 plain characters. The forgery control did not catch it (its marker is longer, and it echoes a real version). The tap now reads only the answer to our own initialize request, and the judge accepts only the specification's revisions, else `other`.

test.name: R-ORC-03: a server cannot put a string of its choosing into protocol_negotiated

records.title: live-probe oracle stage (review, before merge).
records.description: live-probe oracle stage (review, before merge). `runProgram` settled on `close`, which waits for every holder of the client's pipes: an orphaned `docker run` left by a killed client kept it open, so the session's container (on the fixed address) was never removed and the stage overran. Clients and suite runs are now process groups stopped whole at the limit, the session's container is removed at once, and the run settles on exit with a short grace.

test.name: R-ORC-04: a client whose child keeps its pipes open is still stopped at its limit, its whole process group with it, and its container removed at once

records.title: live-probe oracle stage (review, before merge).
records.description: live-probe oracle stage (review, before merge). The SDK clients run on the runner, outside the container's memory limit; a server writing gigabytes without a line break grew their heaps (a runner out-of-memory risk). Each client's server command now goes through `corpus/oracles/relay.mjs`: 24 MiB in all, 4 MiB a line.

test.name: R-ORC-05: what a server can send an oracle client on the runner is capped (relay.mjs): a flood without line breaks is stopped

records.title: live-probe oracle stage (review, before merge).
records.description: live-probe oracle stage (review, before merge). No `finally` around the conformance loop: an error skipped `bridge.close()`, leaving the live session's container on the fixed address while the driver went on; the stage's own cleanup could throw too. The bridge now closes in a `finally`, and cleanup errors are recorded, never thrown.

test.name: R-ORC-06: an error inside the conformance loop still closes the bridge, so no session container is left on the address

records.title: live-probe oracle stage (review, before merge).
records.description: live-probe oracle stage (review, before merge). Client and scenario limits ran to the budget less 5 s, plus up to about 40 s of kill, removal and trace wait, eating the reserve kept for the driver's second probe. Limits now keep 30 s of cleanup inside the budget. Also: the driver read a target without a limit as 300 s (the sandbox's default is 600 s), and HTTP targets got the oracle allowance though the stage never runs for them.

test.name: R-ORC-07: the stage keeps cleanup time inside its budget; the driver reads a target without a limit as 600 s; HTTP targets get no oracle allowance

records.title: live-probe oracle bridge (review, before merge).
records.description: live-probe oracle bridge (review, before merge). One server process at a time was not enforced under concurrent requests: a second initialize arriving while the first closed the open session could start a second container (which then fails on the fixed address). Starting and ending sessions now take turns.

test.name: R-ORC-08: two initialize requests at once still leave one server process

records.title: live-probe oracle judge (review, before merge).
records.description: live-probe oracle judge (review, before merge). A check id repeated within a scenario kept only its first occurrence, so a later FAILURE was dropped and a baseline could pass falsely; a client that crashed (`client_error`) was D6, not D12 as the design and the docstring say. Repeats now take the worst status; a crash is D12.

test.name: R-ORC-09: a check id repeated in a scenario takes its worst status; a client that crashed is D12

records.title: live-probe oracle stage (review, before merge).
records.description: live-probe oracle stage (review, before merge). The self test skipped clients marked `unavailable`, so a run where every client failed to install still passed; and when the clients-only and the full stage both ran for a target, the first one's record was dropped and its time stayed in `probe_ms`. The self test now refuses an unavailable client (the control still tolerates an install outage, recorded as our fault), and both records are kept in raw/ and timed.

test.name: R-ORC-10: the self test refuses a client that did not install; both oracle records of a target are kept and timed
